To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

for a general system with first-order reactions, the second moments are governed by a matrix that is a function only of the network topology; that the steady-state distribution of a system of first-order conversions is Poisson; that the steady state distribution of a system with first-order conversions and diffusion is Gaussian; that the steady states of systems of first-order reactions are stable in the sense that the second moments are monotonically decreasing; that catalytic reactions can increase or decrease the variance of a system component;

(1) the evolution equations for first two moments of the probability density function for a general system can be derived from the governing master equation, (2) the evolution equations are explicitly in terms of network topology, (3) the steady-state distribution for an open system is a Poisson, and (4) the variance is not a good measure for the noise in a system of first-order reaction.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a stochastic model for a system of first-order chemical reactions in which the reactions are of two different types: (1) catalytic reactions and (2) conversion reactions.
stochastic modeling and analysis of chemical reaction systems.
the stochastic analysis of first- order reaction networks and the derivation of the governing master equation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the stochastic model derived herein, which is a generalization of a model derived previously by McQuarrie and Jaeckle, is a powerful tool for the analysis of first-order chemical reaction networks.
the variance in a first-order reaction system is determined by the network topology and the nature of the reactions.

the stochastic behavior of first-order reaction systems is very different from that of higher-order reactions, and the stochastic analysis of first order systems is a subject worthy of much further study.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have derived the master equation for first-order reactions in a manner that allows us to analyze the effects separately of topology, reaction type, and diffusion.

the stochastic analysis of a general system of chemical reactions can be reduced to the analysis of the evolution of the mean values and the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a single matrix, which is the same matrix that appears in the analysis of the deterministic model of the system.

the variance of the components of a general system of coupled first-order reactions is determined by the eigenvalues of a matrix that depends only on the topology of the system, and that this matrix is the same for all reaction types.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the evolution of the second moment of a system of first-order conversions can be represented explicitly as a function of the eigenvalues of the network matrix.
the evolution of the second moment of the distribution is governed by the eigenvalue structure of the mean evolution matrix, and that this structure is determined by the network topology.
the evolution of the moments is governed by the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the mean equation, which in turn is determined by the network topology.
